resources.string: How pancreatic acinar cells release digestive enzymes
A qualitative view of the normal human exocrine pancreas, following digestive proteins from an acinar cell to the duodenum. Structures, timing and particle counts are schematic.
Find an acinus in a pancreatic lobule

A pancreatic lobule contains many small clusters of secretory cells called acini. In each acinus, the broad bases of the cells face outward and the narrow apical ends face a shared lumen that opens into a small duct.

Ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum near the base make digestive proteins. The proteins pass through the Golgi apparatus and are packaged into secretory granules that accumulate near the apical surface.
Release cargo into the acinar lumen
A granule fuses with the apical membrane and empties its contents into the lumen. Amylase is secreted as an active enzyme. Trypsinogen is secreted as an inactive precursor of the enzyme trypsin.
Cargo from several acini flows through branches of the pancreatic duct system. Acinar cells supply the digestive proteins; cells lining the ducts add bicarbonate-rich fluid to the same stream.

The main pancreatic duct delivers pancreatic juice to the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine. There, amylase helps digest starch, and inactive precursors such as trypsinogen can be activated.
